***1. Response to Weakness 1***

We thank the reviewer for these valuable suggestions regarding the presentation and analysis in our paper.

First, we acknowledge that the notation for $L_{\mathrm{FGV}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{FGT}}$ loss was not sufficiently clarified. Specifically, $L_{\mathrm{FGV}}$ denotes the Fine-Grained Visual Learning, and $L_{\mathrm{FGT}}$ denotes the Fine-Grained Textual Learning. We will explicitly define these abbreviations upon their first appearance in Section 3.2.

Second, regarding bilingual capability, an overview of the dataset composition used in both training stages is already provided in Appendix A, and we now additionally include sample examples from the bilingual training data at [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ICLR_RE-1EDD/train_sample.md]. To examine how different data compositions affect the model’s bilingual capability, we conduct an ablation study comparing two variants trained under identical settings except for the data used in Stage 2: one uses English-only data, while the other uses both English and Chinese data. Results in the table below show that the bilingual variant not only achieves higher accuracy on Chinese benchmarks but also consistently improves performance on English-only evaluation sets, confirming a mutually promoting effect between the two languages.

***2. Response to Weakness 2***

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. The effectiveness of the Textual Intra-modal Contrastive (TIC) mechanism is supported by quantitative results in Table 7 of the main paper, which shows that TIC improves performance on fine-grained tasks such as bounding-box classification and fine-grained understanding. 

To further substantiate this claim with direct evidence of improved semantic separability, we additionally conduct an embedding visualization comparing text representations with and without the TIC loss. As shown in the visualization at [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ICLR_RE-1EDD/t2t.md], when TIC is enabled, semantically similar but distinct phrases become better separated in the embedding space. This suggests that TIC indeed enhances semantic separability among fine-grained textual descriptions.

Results in the table below show that the full two-stage model outperforms the Stage-1-only variant, with consistent improvements on benchmarks that require detailed visual-semantic understanding, such as fine-grained understanding and open-vocabulary segmentation. This confirms that Stage 2 effectively enhances fine-grained alignment capabilities.

***1. Response to Weakness 1***

We sincerely thank the reviewer for this comment. Our central view is that true fine-grained vision-language understanding requires simultaneous fine-grained modeling in both vision and language. Visually, it involves recognizing objects, attributes, and their spatial arrangements. Linguistically, it entails distinguishing between semantically close but meaningfully different expressions, such as “striped shirt” versus “checkered shirt.” 

To realize this vision, FG-CLIP 2 builds a unified framework that jointly optimizes three learning objectives: global alignment learning for overall semantic consistency, fine-grained visual learning for detailed region-level representation, and fine-grained textual learning for nuanced linguistic discrimination. On top of this tripartite foundation, we introduce the CMR loss to strengthen the model’s discrimination of semantic boundaries by focusing on hard negatives, and the TIC loss to disentangle semantically similar but distinct region descriptions. In addition, we design a dynamic resolution training strategy that enables the model to adapt to diverse input scales, including low-resolution web images and high-resolution product photos. We also extend the vision encoder with a dense feature module to support pixel-level dense understanding tasks such as open-vocabulary segmentation. These architectural and training innovations collectively enable FG-CLIP 2 to achieve stronger fine-grained capabilities than prior vision-language models.

Building upon this unified fine-grained framework, we extend FG-CLIP 2 to support bilingual fine-grained understanding by training on a carefully curated combination of English and Chinese image-text data. This enables strong fine-grained understanding in Chinese, a capability that is largely absent in existing fine-grained vision-language models. To support systematic evaluation of such bilingual fine-grained models, we further contribute a new Chinese fine-grained benchmark comprising four datasets covering long-caption image-text retrieval and region-based classification, addressing a clear gap in current evaluation resources.

***2. Response to Weakness 2***

We appreciate the reviewer’s point regarding fair comparison. To address this, we conduct additional experiments in which we retrain two representative baselines, SigLIP 2 and Chinese-CLIP, using the same training data in Stage 2 as used for FG-CLIP 2. Due to computational constraints, we train all models, including FG-CLIP 2, using only Stage 2 data without any Stage 1 pretraining, ensuring a fully controlled and fair comparison.

As shown in the table below, even under this constrained setting, FG-CLIP 2 consistently outperforms both SigLIP 2 and Chinese-CLIP across all evaluation benchmarks. The results indicate that while the bilingual data contributes to fine-grained understanding, the architectural design and tailored learning objectives of FG-CLIP 2 deliver substantial additional gains in modeling capability.

| Chinese-CLIP* | ViT-B/16 | 26.9/25.5 | 47.3/31.7 | 48.3/47.7 | 80.0/65.5 | 41.4/69.0 | 16.3/33.0/37.1/73.9 |
| SigLIP 2* | ViT-B/16 | 49.1/49.0 | 71.5/53.5 | 50.5/49.4 | 81.0/52.7 | 53.7/79.7 | 25.5/50.6/59.2/83.4 |
| FG-CLIP 2* | ViT-B/16 | **60.9/62.6** | **72.1/53.7** | **65.9/69.5** | **84.3/66.1** | **71.0/95.4** | **51.9/76.0/80.5/90.6** |

***3. Response to Weakness 3***

We thank the reviewer for raising this concern. In fact, beyond the global alignment learning objective, the weights of the four additional losses (FGV, FGT, CMR, and TIC) were not set arbitrarily. Instead, we performed a systematic ablation study using a sequential tuning strategy: starting from the base global alignment loss, we introduced each additional loss one at a time, tuned its weight while keeping previously added losses fixed (and excluding future ones), and selected the value that maximized average validation performance.

The figure in [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ICLR_RE-1EDD/hyperparameters_ablation.png] shows the average performance curves over different hyperparameter values for each loss, where the average is computed across several representative evaluation tasks: DCI, MSCOCO, DOCCI-CN, Flickr30k-CNA, Bbox Classification (COCO⁸⁰), and Fine-Grained Understanding. To improve transparency and reproducibility, we will include these detailed hyperparameter tuning results in the appendix of the final manuscript.

summary.value: This paper proposes a bilingual fine-grained vision-language alignment model for English and Chinese. It extends CLIP-style architectures by integrating fine-grained supervision signals and introducing a new Textual Intra-modal Contrastive (TIC) loss. The training follows a two-stage paradigm: global alignment with long and short captions, and fine-grained regional alignment using multiple discriminative objectives. Authors curate large-scale bilingual datasets and construct several Chinese benchmarks to evaluate fine-grained and bilingual understanding. Experiments on 29 datasets and 8 tasks show consistent improvements over existing methods in retrieval, detection, segmentation, and as a vision encoder in large multimodal models (LMMs)

strengths.value: This paper proposes a comprehensive bilingual fine-grained vision-language alignment model for English and Chinese. The two-stage training design systematically transitions from global to fine-grained alignment, combining both caption lengths and region-level signals. Explicit bilingual integration with curated English and Chinese datasets totaling over ~2.4 billion pairs supports multilingual robustness. The approach bridges the gap between previously disjoint English fine-grained and Chinese global models, enhancing cross-lingual generalization. The resulted model FG-CLIP2 verified on 29 datasets and 8 tasks shows consistent improvements over existing methods

weaknesses.value:
- The presentation in this paper could be improved, especially in the Approach section. For example, Section 3.2 does not introduce the $L_{FGV}$ and $L_{FGT}$ loss. If these losses are defined in FG-CLIP (or elsewhere), they need be mentioned. In Section 3.3 on training data,  which is the key factor enabling the model’s bilingual capability, the paper lacks essential visualizations and analysis, such as dataset construction details, sample examples, and composition distribution. Moreover, there appears to be no experimental analysis of how different data components contribute to bilingual performance improvement.For example, is there evidence that the inclusion of Chinese training data improves the model’s English alignment capability, given the larger overall training corpus?
- As one of the core contributions, the Textual Intra-modal Contrastive (TIC) mechanism lacks sufficient experimental validation. For instance, no visualization or embedding analysis is provided to support the claimed improvement in semantic separability.
- Similarly, the two-stage training strategy from coarse to fine alignment is not thoroughly evaluated. All results are reported only for the final model, without distinguishing between training stages. Therefore, the claim that the second stage effectively enhances fine-grained capability is insufficiently verified.
- Finally, the comparison with previous works should include the amount of training data used for each model.

questions.value: Section 4.1 mentions that the first-stage training uses ASCEND 910B NPUs, while the second stage uses H800 GPUs. How long did each stage cost, and why was the second-stage training not continued on NPUs?

***1. Response to Weakness 1***

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. The performance gain of FG-CLIP 2 over FG-CLIP stems from multiple synergistic improvements, which we analyze below.

While SigLIP 2 provides a stronger foundation than CLIP, it still exhibits limited fine-grained capabilities. For example, on tasks such as fine-grained understanding and bounding box classification, its performance remains modest, as shown in Table 1 of the manuscript. To address this, FG-CLIP 2 introduces several key components specifically designed for fine-grained vision-language alignment. It employs fine-grained visual learning to obtain detailed region-level representations, and fine-grained textual learning to support nuanced linguistic discrimination. We introduce the CMR loss to strengthen the model’s ability to distinguish semantic boundaries by focusing on hard negative examples, and the TIC loss to disentangle region descriptions that are semantically similar but conceptually distinct. In addition, we adopt a dynamic resolution training strategy to effectively handle images at diverse scales. Furthermore, the effectiveness of these components is supported by our carefully curated training data, which provides high-quality supervision for fine-grained vision-language alignment. This data design plays an important complementary role in realizing the full potential of our architecture.

Regarding bilingual training, we conduct an ablation study comparing two variants trained under identical settings except for the data used in Stage 2: one uses English-only data, while the other uses both English and Chinese data. The results show that the bilingual variant not only achieves higher accuracy on Chinese benchmarks but also consistently improves performance on English-only evaluation sets. This confirms a mutually promoting effect between the two languages during joint training.

| Method | Backbone | DCI | MSCOCO | DOCCI-CN | Flickr30k-CNA | COCO⁸⁰ | Fine-Grained Understanding |
|--------|----------|:---:|:------:|:-----:|:-------------:|:-----------:|:--------------------------:|
| | | I→T/T→I | I→T/T→I |  I→T/T→I | I→T/T→I | Top-1/Top-5 | Hard/Medium/Easy/Trivial |

| FG-CLIP 2 | ViT-B/16 | 64.5/64.9 | 72.1/54.5 | 71.2/75.4 | 85.4/69.9 | 74.9/95.7 | 52.3/76.3/80.3/92.0 |

***2. Response to Weakness 2***

We thank the reviewer for raising this concern. In fact, beyond the global alignment learning objective, the weights of the four additional losses (FGV, FGT, CMR, and TIC) were not set arbitrarily. Instead, we performed a systematic ablation study using a sequential tuning strategy: starting from the base global alignment loss, we introduced each additional loss one at a time, tuned its weight while keeping previously added losses fixed (and excluding future ones), and selected the value that maximized average validation performance.

The figure in [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ICLR_RE-1EDD/hyperparameters_ablation.png] shows the average performance curves over different hyperparameter values for each loss, where the average is computed across several representative evaluation tasks: DCI, MSCOCO, DOCCI-CN, Flickr30k-CNA, Bbox Classification (COCO⁸⁰), and Fine-Grained Understanding. To improve transparency and reproducibility, we will include these detailed hyperparameter tuning results in the appendix of the final manuscript.

Importantly, the CMR and TIC losses are specifically designed to enhance fine-grained semantic discrimination, and their benefits are most pronounced on tasks that require region-level or attribute-aware understanding, such as bounding box classification and fine-grained understanding. On benchmarks like Flickr30k and ImageNet-V2, which primarily rely on global image-text matching or category-level recognition, the contribution of these fine-grained objectives is comparatively smaller. This explains why the ablation results in Table 7 show clear gains on COCO⁸⁰ and FG-OVD, but more modest improvements on Flickr30k and ImageNet-V2. These trends align well with the design goals of our method.

summary.value: This paper designs a bilingual vision-language model to enhance fine-grained alignment between visual content and linguistic descriptions for both English and Chinese. It adopts a two-stage training paradigm with multiple discriminative objectives and is trained on large-scale bilingual datasets, outperforming existing models across 29 datasets and 8 tasks.

Dear Area Chair,

We sincerely appreciate the reviewers' insightful comments and constructive feedback on our manuscript. We have thoroughly addressed all concerns raised by the reviewers, and we believe these revisions have significantly strengthened the paper. Below is a concise summary of our key responses:

**For Reviewer ipHB:**

- As initially presented in the original manuscript, we stated our focus on building a bilingual fine-grained vision-language alignment model and discussed the distinctions between FG-CLIP 2 and previous fine-grained vision-language models. We have further reinforced this clarification by explicitly elaborating on our central contribution, architectural innovations, and training objective innovations. We specifically addressed how these innovations enable enhanced fine-grained semantic discrimination, responding to the reviewer's concern about our methodological differentiation.
- While using different large-scale pretraining data is common in this field (e.g., MetaCLIP 2 and SigLIP 2), we conducted additional experiments retraining baselines on identical data specifically to address the reviewer's concern, demonstrating FG-CLIP 2's consistent superiority.
- We provided detailed hyperparameter tuning results through systematic ablation studies, showing how we determined the optimal weights for each loss component.

**For Reviewer XDPh:**

- We identified that the performance improvement stems from multiple synergistic components (fine-grained visual/textual learning, CMR/TIC losses, dynamic resolution training), not merely from SigLIP 2 initialization or bilingual data alone. We added new ablation experiments confirming the mutually promoting effect between the two languages during joint training.
- We included comprehensive hyperparameter tuning results in the appendix, addressing the concern about loss weight settings. Regarding the Table 7 ablation results, we clarified that the TIC and CMR losses are specifically designed to enhance fine-grained semantic discrimination, hence showing significant improvements on COCO⁸⁰ and FG-OVD (fine-grained tasks), while having smaller effects on Flickr30k and ImageNet-V2 (global image-level tasks).
- We have added a detailed comparison with UMG-CLIP (ECCV 2024) and Contrastive Localized Language-Image Pre-Training (ICML 2025), based on the results reported in their publications since their models are not publicly available.

**For Reviewer HrUG:**

- We have clarified the loss abbreviations as requested. The data composition was initially presented in Appendix A, and we've added additional data examples to the appendix. We also conducted extra experiments proving bilingual data enhances English alignment performance.
- We included quantitative ablation results in the original manuscript demonstrating TIC's effectiveness. To address the reviewer's concern, we have added embedding visualizations showing TIC's improvement in semantic separability.
- We evaluated the Stage 1 model separately, showing consistent improvements from Stage 2 on fine-grained tasks.
- We added a table comparing training data volumes across different methods and addressed the hardware question regarding NPU/GPU usage in Stage 1 vs. Stage 2.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Best regards,

488's authors.

We thank the reviewer for this question. Training times increase with model size: Stage 1 takes 88, 175, and 254 hours on 160 ASCEND 910B NPUs for ViT-B, ViT-L, and ViT-So respectively, while Stage 2 takes 8, 16, and 24 hours on 16 H800 GPUs for the same models. 

The switch to H800 GPUs in Stage 2 is due to precision limitations of the RoI-Align operator on ASCEND NPUs. As stated in the “Constraint Notes” at [https://www.hiascend.com/document/detail/zh/Pytorch/720/apiref/torchnpuCustomsapi/context/%EF%BC%88beta%EF%BC%89torch_npu-npu_roi_align.md], the NPU implementation of RoI-Align matches the NumPy reference in forward computation, but exhibits numerical discrepancies in the backward pass compared to the CUDA version. These gradient inaccuracies can adversely affect the stability and convergence of fine-grained alignment training, which relies heavily on precise region-level gradients. H800 GPUs provide a numerically robust implementation that ensures reliable training.

summary.value:
This paper proposes a FG-CLIP 2, a fine-grained CLIP for English and Chinese. The claim contributions include “a recipe” for training bilingual CLIP with long and region-based captions with comprehensive experiments to show its effectiveness. Another contribution is a benchmark for Chinese multimodal understanding. Model, code, and benchmark are/will be released.

This paper receives ratings of 4, 6, 6. Reviewers find the bilinguality direction well-motivated, and appreciate the engineering efforts (data, modeling, and benchmarking) that lead to a highly capable model with evidence of strong performance. On the other hand, the main criticism is that it is unclear which factors lead to performance gains (SigLIP 2 for initialization, curated Chinese data, loss functions, etc.) due to various components being introduced.

reviewer_concerns.value:
In response to the reviews, in addition to pointing the reviewers to the results in the paper, the authors present ablation experiments, including comparing previous approaches trained on the same data, understanding effect of Chinese training data in stage 2, presenting visualization curves for hyperparameter optimization of the weights of the proposed loss functions.

These results help alleviate the reviewers' concern but not entirely given multiple proposed components. In the end, the authors’ claim can only be as specific as “the performance improvement stems from multiple synergistic components (fine-grained visual/textual learning, CMR/TIC losses, dynamic resolution training), not merely from SigLIP 2 initialization or bilingual data alone” which does not provide significant insights about which factors contribute most. While the current results do seem to show the benefit of each proposed component, the paper would benefit from 1) better justifying why these components and their combination are significant (especially with respect to the existing work) and 2) re-organizing the results with clearer takeaways.
